title: Polpo alla luciana
subtitle: Neapolitan braised octopus in tomato sauce
excerpt: Polpo alla luciana is the octopus braise of Naples: whole octopus slow-cooked in a covered terracotta pot with tomato, garlic, olive oil, and chilli, entirely in its own liquid. The octopus releases moisture as it cooks; nothing extra is added. The result is tender, intensely flavoured octopus in a concentrated tomato sauce.
sourceNotes: Neapolitan coastal recipe from the Santa Lucia district. Polpo alla luciana is associated with the fishermen's quarter near the Castel dell'Ovo in Naples. Method drawn from Jeanne Caròla Francesconi, La cucina napoletana (1965), and traditional Neapolitan seafood preparations.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make a day ahead; the octopus becomes even more tender overnight. Reheat gently.

glossaryTerms.definition: Neapolitan style of cooking octopus in a sealed vessel with no added liquid, so it steams in its own juices; the name comes from the Santa Lucia district of Naples, historically a fishermen's quarter.

content.text: is an octopus sealed into a pot with tomato, garlic, oil, capers, and chilli. Nothing else is added. No water, no wine. The octopus releases its own liquid as it cooks, creating a briny, concentrated sauce entirely from itself. The key is a very tight-fitting lid and patience: the first 15 minutes are at high heat to start the process; then low heat for 45 minutes without lifting the lid.

items.prepNote: cleaned, head and beak removed by fishmonger; leave tentacles whole if possible

content.text: Put {{octopus}} of cleaned octopus into a heavy casserole. Add {{extra-virgin-olive-oil}} of olive oil, {{tinned-tomatoes}} of crushed tomatoes, {{garlic}} of garlic, {{capers}} of capers, {{olives-black}} of black olives, and {{chilli-flakes}} of chilli flakes. Do not add any liquid.

Cover very tightly (if the lid is not tight, seal it with a layer of foil underneath). Set over high heat for 5 minutes. The pot should be hissing. Reduce to the lowest possible heat. Cook for 50 minutes without lifting the lid.

Lift the lid after 50 minutes. The octopus should be tender: a skewer should slide in without resistance. Rest for 10 minutes. Taste the sauce for salt; it may need very little as the octopus and capers are salty. Scatter with parsley. Serve with crusty bread or over polenta.

items.symptom: Octopus is still tough after 50 minutes
items.cause: Heat was too high during the slow phase, or the octopus was very large.
items.fix: Continue cooking. Octopus toughens before it tenderises; at 60 to 70 minutes of total cooking it should yield. If still firm, continue for another 20 minutes.

items.symptom: Pot is dry when you lift the lid
items.cause: Lid was not tight enough and steam escaped.
items.fix: Add a small splash of water and continue cooking. Next time, use foil under the lid to create a tighter seal.

content.text: Polpo alla luciana takes its name from Santa Lucia, the Naples waterfront where octopus fishermen once lived. The method of cooking octopus in a sealed dry pot with no added liquid is specific to this dish and to Naples; elsewhere, octopus goes into wine or water. The traditional vessel was a terracotta testo. A cast-iron casserole with a tight lid gives the same result.
